h1:
Chiang Mai Street Food
Market by Market
intro: One of the best things about Chiang Mai is that you can eat your way through the whole day and never repeat yourself. Wake up early for khanom jeen and patongo at Kad Luang, pick up sai ua and crispy pork as gifts in the afternoon, then settle in for stewed pork leg over rice at Pratu Chang Phueak come evening — and cap a Sunday off with a Walking Street that runs the better part of a kilometre. We've sorted out which market does what, which stalls draw a queue, when they open, and how much cash to bring.

blocks.html: Chiang Mai's street food isn't all in one place — it splits into clear neighbourhoods. Kad Luang is the daytime market for northern dishes and edible souvenirs. Pratu Chiang Mai and Pratu Chang Phueak are the evening markets where people who work in town come to eat for real. And the Sunday Walking Street is the big weekend event that pulls everything together onto a single road. We'll walk you through each one and tell you straight which are worth the trip and which get crowded enough that you'll need some patience.

blocks.text: Kad Luang (Warorot Market) — northern food and souvenirs in one spot

blocks.html: Kad Luang, officially Warorot Market, is the oldest and largest market in town, sitting along the Ping River near Nawarat Bridge. Locals call it "Kad Luang," which literally means "big market." The ground floor is the food and northern-dishes zone, while the upper floor sells clothes, shoes and bags. The indoor market runs roughly 05:00–18:00 daily, and the night market in the side lanes kicks off around 5pm and goes until about 10pm. This is the best place to come if you want to take home sai ua (northern sausage), crispy pork rinds or nam prik num — there are loads of stalls and prices run lower than the souvenir shops in the malls.

items.name: Damrong — sai ua + fried pork (Kad Luang)
items.blurb: A Kad Luang institution, sitting in the middle of the ground-floor food zone with a queue at almost any hour. The sai ua comes out steaming and fragrant with herbs, and the fried pork is full chunks of meat in a crisp batter, crunchy outside and tender inside. Easy to grab as a gift to take home.

items.name: Khanom jeen nam ngiao, Kad Luang
items.blurb: The market's signature dish: rice noodles under an orange nam ngiao broth coloured with red kapok flowers, gently sour, with minced pork and blood cubes. Eaten with crispy pork and fresh vegetables — this is what northerners actually have for breakfast.

items.name: Patongo Ko Neng
items.blurb: A patongo (Thai dough fritter) stall listed in the Michelin Guide, fried into shapes like dragons, dinosaurs and elephants — crisp outside, fluffy inside. Dip them in pandan custard or condensed milk. Kids love the shapes, adults love the crunch.

items.name: Big Brother Song fish-ball noodles
items.blurb: An old Chinese noodle shop run by one family for over 75 years, known for its handmade fish balls — some shaped into hearts. The broth is clear and well-rounded, an old-school flavour that's getting hard to find.

blocks.title: Kad Luang tips
blocks.html: Parking around here is scarce and tight. If you're staying in the old city, taking a songthaew (red truck) or just walking is easier than driving yourself. Most stalls take cash only, so bring small notes.

blocks.text: Pratu Chiang Mai (the gate market) — where locals really eat

blocks.html: Pratu Chiang Mai is the south gate of the old moat, and the market sits on Bamrungburi Road — two markets in one spot. Before dawn it's a fresh market for residents, then from 5pm until midnight it transforms into a full-street street-food market. The draw is that it's a locals' market that tourists only caught onto later, so prices are still local prices. There's savoury food, sweets, fruit, smoothies, even vegetarian options. The best time is around 6pm, when all the stalls are open but it isn't too packed yet.

items.name: Khao mok gai, Pratu Chiang Mai
items.blurb: A well-known stall in the market: rice cooked yellow with turmeric, topped with fried shallots, served with pickled cucumber and onion and a sharp green dipping sauce. People go out of their way to come eat this.

items.name: Grilled chicken · som tam · sticky rice
items.blurb: The evening market's favourite Isan combo: grilled chicken with crispy skin, som tam pounded to order, and a side of hot sticky rice. A filling dinner that's great value for a few baht.

items.name: Pad thai · oyster omelette on the hot griddle
items.blurb: Stir-fried fresh right at the front of the stall — you catch the smell of the wok as you pass. Add shrimp or egg if you like. A snack you won't walk by without grabbing.

blocks.title: What to know about the gate market
blocks.html: Seating here is limited and a lot of stalls bag everything up to eat while you walk. If you want to sit comfortably, go early in the evening before the crowds — and bring small cash notes, same as every market here.

blocks.text: Pratu Chang Phueak — the cowboy-hat lady's pork-leg rice

blocks.html: North of Pratu Chiang Mai is Pratu Chang Phueak. The food market in front of this gate opens in the evening from around 5pm, but what made it famous worldwide is a single stall — "Khao Kha Moo Chang Phueak," run by the lady in the cowboy hat, which has been written up in the Michelin Guide. Pork leg stewed until it's falling-apart tender, ladled over rice with a five-spice egg, eaten with pickled mustard greens and a garlic-chilli dipping sauce. There's a queue for it every evening.

items.name: Khao Kha Moo Chang Phueak (the cowboy-hat lady)
items.blurb: A Chiang Mai street-food legend: pork leg stewed so long it melts in your mouth, ladled over hot rice with a five-spice egg and pickled mustard greens. In the Michelin Guide, with a queue almost every evening — and it sells out fast.

items.name: Sweets and desserts at Pratu Chang Phueak
items.blurb: After the pork leg, a few steps on you'll find dessert carts with bua loy, khanom krok, roti and smoothies — an easy way to close out dinner.

blocks.title: If you're after the cowboy-hat lady's pork leg
blocks.html: It sells out fast — go before 6pm and be ready to queue. Show up late and it may be gone. The stall is on the inner side of Pratu Chang Phueak; just look for the sign and the long line.

blocks.text: Sunday Walking Street (Ratchadamnoen) — the big weekend event

blocks.html: Every Sunday evening, Ratchadamnoen Road in the old city — from Tha Phae Gate down to Wat Phra Singh — closes to traffic and becomes the Walking Street, running roughly 4pm to midnight. It's the most crowded market in Chiang Mai, with food, crafts, clothes and live music in stretches. The food runs from khao soi, sai ua and grilled pork skewers to khanom buang yuan and mango sticky rice, plus oddities like fried insects. Most things are ฿20–50 a skewer or piece. The peak crush is around 7pm to 9pm — if you want room to walk, come between 4 and 5pm.

blocks.title: There's a weekday walking street too
blocks.html: If you can't make it on a Sunday, Saturday evening has the Wua Lai Walking Street in the Wua Lai neighbourhood, focused on silverware and the same kind of food. It's a touch less crowded than the Sunday one.

faq.q: Where's the best place for street food in Chiang Mai?
faq.a: It depends on the time and your style. If you come in the daytime and want northern souvenirs, go to Kad Luang (Warorot Market). If you come in the evening and want to eat like a local, head to the Pratu Chiang Mai or Pratu Chang Phueak markets. And on a Sunday evening, don't miss the Ratchadamnoen Walking Street, which pulls everything together onto a single road.

faq.q: What time do the Pratu Chiang Mai and Pratu Chang Phueak markets open?
faq.a: Both are evening markets, opening from around 5pm onward and running late. The best window is around 6pm, when all the stalls are open but it isn't packed yet. Famous stalls like the cowboy-hat lady's pork-leg rice at Pratu Chang Phueak sell out fast, so go before 6pm.

faq.q: What souvenirs is Kad Luang good for?
faq.a: Sai ua (northern sausage), crispy pork rinds, nam prik num, nam prik ong and all sorts of northern dried goods. Well-known stalls like Damrong have sai ua and fried pork, and you can ask for vacuum-sealed bags if you're flying. Prices at Kad Luang are usually lower than the souvenir shops in the malls.

faq.q: Do Chiang Mai street-food markets take cards?
faq.a: Most take cash only, so carry small notes of ฿20–100. Some stalls accept PromptPay transfers, but the signal can be slow when it's busy — cash is the easiest.

faq.q: Is the Sunday Walking Street on every day?
faq.a: The Ratchadamnoen Walking Street runs only on Sunday evenings. On Saturday evenings there's the Wua Lai Walking Street in the Wua Lai neighbourhood instead, focused on silverware and food, and a little less crowded than the Sunday one.
